opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting and underappreciated parts of the whole story. A lot of the conversation around AI in drug discovery focuses on the front end: can we find a molecule faster, can we cut the time from target to candidate from years to months. That matters, but if you look at where the time, cost and failure in the pipeline actually sit, it's overwhelmingly in the clinic. Most drugs that enter clinical trials fail, and they often fail for reasons we could in principle have anticipated: the molecule hits something it shouldn't, the toxicity profile isn't what we hoped, or the biology of the target in real patients is different from what we assumed.

So the real promise isn't just making molecules faster. It's making better molecules, ones we understand much more deeply before they ever go into a person. If you have models that can reason about how a compound interacts not just with its intended target but across the proteome, and predict properties like selectivity, metabolism and potential off-target effects, then you're going into the clinic with far more confidence. Ideally that shows up as higher success rates per trial, and that's where the economics of the whole industry change.

Longer term, I think it changes how we design trials too. If you understand the mechanism at a much finer level, you can be more precise about which patients are likely to respond, which biomarkers to track, and what dose ranges make sense. Trials can become more targeted and more informative. And there's a really nice feedback loop: everything we learn in the clinic flows back into the models and makes the next round of design better.

I'd be careful not to overpromise. Biology is enormously complex, and the clinic is the ultimate ground truth. There's no shortcut around proving safety and efficacy in people, nor should there be. But I think we're moving from a world where clinical development is largely a high-stakes bet to one where it's more of a confirmation of something we've already understood quite deeply computationally. If we can get there, it opens up the ability to go after diseases and targets that have historically been considered too risky or too hard, and that's ultimately what gets me most excited.

r001.rationale: The response proposes modeling a compound’s interactions across the proteome and predicting selectivity, metabolism, and off-target effects before it enters clinical trials.

r002.rationale: It says deeper understanding of a drug’s mechanism could make trials more targeted and informative, including more precise patient selection, biomarkers, and dose ranges.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most of the attention right now goes to the discovery side, the "can a model design a molecule" question, and that's actually the part I worry about least. The thing that really determines whether a drug reaches a patient is what happens after you've got a candidate. Clinical development is where the time goes, it's where the money goes, and it's where the vast majority of programs die. Something like ninety percent of what enters the clinic never comes out the other end as an approved medicine.

So when I think about AI-designed drugs changing clinical development, I think about it in a few layers.

The first is just the quality of what you put in. If you've designed a molecule with a model that has a real understanding of the biology, of selectivity, of how it behaves in a human body rather than just a dish, then you're starting the clinical journey with a much better prior. A lot of late-stage failures are really early-stage mistakes that took years to reveal themselves. Better design should mean fewer of those surprises at Phase 2 and Phase 3.

The second layer is patient selection. Many drugs don't fail because the mechanism is wrong, they fail because they were tested in the wrong population. If the same models that design the molecule can also tell you which patients are most likely to respond, you can run smaller, faster trials with a much clearer signal. That's a huge shift in the economics.

And then the third layer, which I think is the most speculative but also the most exciting, is this idea of the trial itself becoming part of the learning loop. Today a trial is a one-shot bet. You design it, you run it for years, you get a readout. I think we'll move toward something more iterative, where data coming back from the clinic feeds directly into the next design decision, and where you can simulate a lot of the outcomes before you ever dose a person. That doesn't replace the trial, you still need real evidence in real humans, but it changes what the trial is for. It becomes a confirmation step rather than a discovery step.

If you put all that together, the vision isn't that AI makes clinical development a bit cheaper. It's that it makes the whole pipeline less of a lottery. And for patients, that's the thing that matters.

r001.rationale: The response says better models could understand a molecule’s selectivity and behavior in the human body, but it does not clearly propose incorporating predictions of the molecule’s effects elsewhere in the body into clinical development.

r002.rationale: It describes AI-informed, iterative trials that use clinical data and simulated outcomes, shifting trials toward confirmation rather than discovery—a fundamental change in how they are conducted.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is to change the quality of the molecules that enter clinical development. Can we design a drug that has the effect we want, reaches the right tissue, and avoids effects we don’t want? Those properties matter enormously once you start testing in people.

If AI helps us get more of those decisions right up front, we could see fewer failures and more effective medicines reaching patients. It could also make it practical to pursue targets that have been very difficult to develop drugs against.

But designing a promising molecule isn’t the same as demonstrating that a medicine works. You still need clinical trials to establish safety and efficacy. The exciting possibility is that we enter those trials with better candidates and a clearer hypothesis about which patients will benefit.

r001.rationale: The response mentions designing molecules to reach the right tissue and avoid unwanted effects, but does not clearly propose incorporating AI predictions of effects elsewhere in the body into clinical development.

r002.rationale: It says AI could bring better candidates and clearer patient hypotheses into trials, while trials remain necessary. It does not suggest that AI-derived knowledge of how molecules work would fundamentally change how human trials are conducted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is to change the quality of the molecules that enter clinical development. A drug has to do many things simultaneously: it has to affect the biology you care about, reach the right tissue, and have an acceptable safety profile. If we can use AI to design against those requirements together, we have a chance to produce better candidates, rather than simply produce candidates faster.

But designing a molecule isn’t the same as demonstrating that it helps patients. You still need clinical trials. The exciting possibility is that we can make more informed bets going into those trials, learn from the results, and feed that understanding back into the next round of design. Ultimately, the measure of success is whether more of those molecules become medicines that make a meaningful difference.

r001.rationale: The response mentions designing for an acceptable safety profile and reaching the right tissue, but does not propose incorporating AI predictions of effects elsewhere in the body into clinical development.

r002.rationale: It says AI could inform candidate selection and learning between design rounds, but does not suggest that greater knowledge of how molecules work would fundamentally change how human trials are conducted.
